text:
Help me write a case for my promotion. I'm the assistant front office manager at a 180-room hotel, and the front office manager job is open. I'm applying, and my general manager wants it in writing by Friday.

Facts:
- I've worked here 6 years, the last 2 as assistant manager.
- Our guest score for check-in on the main review site went from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and all the rooms were renovated during the same time.
- I rewrote the front desk training. New hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.
- Front desk turnover was 9 of 14 people in the year before I became assistant manager, and 5 of 14 last year.
- I've covered the front office manager's job alone for the 7 weeks since she left.
- I have never managed a budget. The front office manager owns a $1.1 million payroll budget.

I want it to say I'm the main reason our guest scores went up. One page.

Before I write it, there's one problem with the guest-score claim I want to flag, plus a few questions.

**The guest-score claim**

- **What you want to say:** you're the main reason the check-in score went from 7.9 to 8.6.
- **What your facts support:** the score rose while you were rewriting training and cutting turnover. But the lobby and every room were renovated over the same 18 months. Your GM approved that renovation and will think of it the moment they read "main reason."
- **What the GM will think:** "New lobby, new rooms. Of course scores went up." Your facts only partly answer that. The score is specifically for check-in, which is your team's work, but the lobby is where check-in happens. If you claim the main credit, the GM may start doubting the rest of the page, and the rest of the page is strong.
- **A version your facts do support:** "The check-in score rose from 7.9 to 8.6. The renovation helped, but check-in is a staff interaction, and over the same period I cut desk turnover from 64% to 36% and had new hires working alone in 5 shifts instead of 9. Guests are being checked in by a more experienced, steadier team." This gives you a real share of the credit without a claim the GM can knock down.

**Your actual strengths.** Lead with these, not the score:
- **Turnover went from 9 of 14 to 5 of 14.** That's 64% down to 36%, nearly cut in half. It's also your best answer on the budget, because every person who doesn't quit is a hire and a round of training you don't pay for.
- **New hires work alone after 5 shifts instead of 9.** That's 44% less training time for each new hire.
- **You've done the job alone for 7 weeks.** That's the closest thing the GM has to a trial run.

**The budget gap.** The GM will raise it, so the page should answer it rather than skip it. My plan is to show the payroll impact you've already had through turnover and training time, then propose a concrete step, such as reviewing the payroll budget with the GM or the controller monthly for your first quarter.

**Questions that could make the case stronger:**
1. Do you know roughly when the renovation finished? If the check-in score was rising before it was done, that's real evidence for your claim and I can make it stronger.
2. Do you have other scores from the same site, like rooms or cleanliness? If check-in rose more than those, that also helps.
3. During the 7 weeks, have you done any payroll work, like scheduling, approving overtime or tracking labor costs? Even a little closes part of the budget gap.
4. Anything from those 7 weeks worth naming, such as a problem you handled, a busy stretch, or a staffing fix?

Tell me which version of the guest-score claim you want, the bold one or the qualified one, and answer whatever questions you can. Then I'll write the one-page memo.

Qualified version is fine. I know the renovation overlapped, so I'm okay just saying what I did.

1. I don't know when it finished. It started 5 months into the 18 months, and the check-in score had already gone from 7.9 to 8.2 before it started.
2. I don't know the other scores.
3. Overtime came in under the monthly plan for the 7 weeks I've covered.
4. No front desk shift went uncovered in those 7 weeks.

Here's the memo. The new detail about timing helps you a lot. The score had already climbed from 7.9 to 8.2 before construction started, so almost half the gain (0.3 of the 0.7) can't be put down to the renovation. That lets you claim a real share of the credit without overstating it.

<final_document>
**To:** [General Manager's name]
**From:** [Your name], Assistant Front Office Manager
**Date:** [Date]
**Re:** My application for Front Office Manager

I'm applying for the Front Office Manager position. For the past seven weeks I've been doing this job alone, and I'd like to make the case that I should keep doing it.

**I've already been running the department.** Since our Front Office Manager left seven weeks ago, I've handled the role alone. No front desk shift has gone uncovered in that time, and overtime has come in under the monthly plan every month.

**I've made the team more stable.** In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk staff left, which is 64%. Last year 5 of 14 left, or 36%. That's close to half the turnover. I also rewrote the front desk training, so new hires now work the desk alone after 5 shifts instead of 9. That's 44% less training time for each new hire, and fewer new hires to train in the first place.

**Guests have noticed.** Our check-in score on [review site] rose from 7.9 to 8.6 over the last 18 months. The lobby and room renovation clearly helped, and I'm not claiming that gain for myself. But the score had already risen from 7.9 to 8.2 in the five months before construction began. Check-in is a conversation between a guest and someone at our desk. Over this period, that person has more often been someone experienced who stayed, and who was ready to work alone sooner.

**The budget.** I haven't owned a budget, and the $1.1 million payroll budget is the largest responsibility in this role. My work so far has been payroll work in practice. Lower turnover means fewer hires and fewer paid training shifts, and overtime has stayed under plan while I've covered the role. To close the gap formally, I'd like to review the payroll budget with you [or the controller] every month for my first quarter. By the end of it, I'd expect to be running the budget on my own.

**Why me rather than an outside hire.** An outside candidate would need months to learn this hotel, this team and our guests. I'd start on day one with a team I trained, results that are already showing, and seven weeks of proof that I can run the department.

Thank you for considering me. I'm glad to talk through any of this before you decide.

[Your name]
</final_document>

A few notes:
- **Placeholders:** fill in the GM's name, the review site, the date and your name. In the budget section, keep "or the controller" only if your hotel has one.
- **Payroll savings:** if you can find what a new hire costs to recruit and train, even a rough number, add it next to the turnover figures. Four fewer departures a year multiplied by a real cost is the strongest answer to the budget question. I left it out because I didn't want to invent a figure.
- **Length:** it fits on one page at normal font size.
